lessons.0.slides.1.title: Where is Burgundy?
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Burgundy lies in eastern France, beginning some 300 km south-east of Paris and stretching about 230 km north to south. It is one of the world's most prestigious wine regions.

lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Spans roughly 230 km from Chablis in the north to Beaujolais in the south
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Close to the Swiss border and influenced by the Alps

lessons.0.slides.3.points.1: Summer: warm but not hot (22–25 °C), allowing slow ripening
lessons.0.slides.3.points.2: Autumn: cool and dry, preserving the grape's freshness and acidity
lessons.0.slides.3.points.3: Winter: cold (down to −5 °C), the vines lie dormant

lessons.0.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.0.question: Which element is most central to Burgundy's all-important concept of terroir?
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.0.options.1: B. The combination of soil, climate and topography
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.0.options.2: C. Whether it was a good vintage
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: Burgundian terroir is the combined influence of soil, climate, topography and sun exposure. It sits at the heart of Burgundy's wine philosophy and explains why each Climat tastes different.
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.1.question: In which part of France is Burgundy located?
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.1.options.2: C. East-central, with a continental climate
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.1.options.3: D. North, near the English Channel
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: Burgundy lies in east-central France with a classic continental climate — hot summers, cold winters and large diurnal swings — ideal for retaining acidity and sugar to build refined, fine-grained wines.
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.2.question: Which of these are key geographic features of Burgundy's vineyards? (multiple answers)
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.2.options.0: A. The slopes of the Côte d'Or
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.2.options.1: B. Soils mixing limestone and clay
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.2.options.2: C. A maritime climate close to the Atlantic
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: The Côte d'Or escarpment, limestone-clay soils and east-facing exposures are all defining features. Burgundy is continental, not maritime — it lies far from the Atlantic.
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.3.question: Which is Burgundy's most important river?
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: The Saône flows along Burgundy's eastern edge, moderating temperatures across the region, mitigating frost risk, and historically serving as a vital trade route for Burgundian wine.
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.4.question: Which climatic features shape Burgundy's wine style? (multiple answers)
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.4.options.0: A. Continental climate with large temperature swings
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.4.options.1: B. Spring frost and hail are the principal natural hazards
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.4.options.2: C. Warm and dry year-round, like the Mediterranean
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.4.options.3: D. A relatively cool climate with a long ripening period
lessons.0.slides.6.questions.4.explanati: Burgundy's continental climate brings spring frost and hail as the main risks, while cooler temperatures lengthen the ripening period and preserve acidity. It is decidedly not a Mediterranean climate.
lessons.0.slides.7.title: Why Terroir Matters
lessons.0.slides.7.content: Burgundy's distinguishing feature is its terroir concept — the same grape variety can express dramatically different styles from one parcel to another, shaped by soil, aspect, altitude and microclimate.
lessons.1.title: History and Monastic Heritage
lessons.1.slides.0.title: History and Monastic Heritage
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 — 20 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: From the Roman era to today, explore two thousand years of Burgundian winemaking and the wisdom of its monks.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: 📅 Burgundy Wine History Timeline
lessons.1.slides.1.note: Suggested visual timeline graphic with historical images and illustrations.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.0.title: Roman Era
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.0.event: The Romans plant the first vines in Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.0.descriptio: The Romans introduced advanced viticulture, laying the foundations of Burgundian wine.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.1.title: Christianisation
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.1.event: Clovis I converts to Christianity; the Church begins to own vineyards
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.1.descriptio: The Church became the principal patron of wine production, with wine essential to the celebration of Mass.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.2.title: Cluny Abbey
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.2.descriptio: One of Europe's most influential abbeys, Cluny became a powerful force advancing both winemaking and quality.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.3.title: Birth of the Cistercians
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.3.descriptio: The disciplined Cistercians pioneered the concept of terroir and created legendary vineyards such as Clos de Vougeot.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.4.title: Spreading Renown
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.4.event: The papacy moves to Avignon; Burgundy wines reach the Curia
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.4.descriptio: Burgundy became the wine of choice at the papal court, sending its international reputation soaring.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.5.title: Varietal Revolution
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.5.event: Duke Philip the Bold of Burgundy bans the planting of Gamay
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.5.descriptio: A historic decision: Pinot Noir is mandated, cementing the quality foundation of Burgundian red wine.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.6.title: The Revolution
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.6.event: The French Revolution: vineyards are nationalised and broken up for sale
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.6.descriptio: Church estates were seized, creating Burgundy's distinctive small-grower landscape.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.7.title: Age of Classification
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.7.descriptio: Burgundy chose a different path, developing a classification philosophy centred on the parcel of land itself.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.8.title: Birth of the AOC
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.8.event: France formally establishes the AOC (controlled designation of origin) system
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.8.descriptio: Burgundy's Climats and concept of terroir gained legal protection.
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.9.title: World Heritage
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.9.event: Burgundy's Climats are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List
lessons.1.slides.1.timeline.9.descriptio: The singularity of 1,247 parcels gained international recognition, safeguarding a millennium of winemaking culture.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🏛️ Roman Origins (from 312 CE)
lessons.1.slides.2.content: After the Roman conquest of Gaul, viticulture was introduced to Burgundy. The Romans recognised that the limestone soils and continental climate were ideally suited to the vine and established the earliest vineyards. Many of today's top sites were already identified as superior in Roman times.
lessons.1.slides.3.title: ⛪ The Medieval Monastic Era (910–1789)
lessons.1.slides.3.content: In the Middle Ages, Catholic monasteries became the heart of winemaking. Monks needed wine for the Mass and saw vinification as work that glorified God. With time and resources for sustained observation and experiment, they gradually built a scientific framework for viticulture and winemaking.
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🏰 The Cistercian Contribution
lessons.1.slides.4.content: The Cistercian monks made an immense contribution to Burgundian wine. Splitting from the Benedictines in 1098 under the motto ora et labora — pray and work — the Cistercians worked their vineyards by hand. With scientific rigour they observed the differences between parcels, originated the concept of terroir, and set strict quality standards.
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Five Monastic Innovations
lessons.1.slides.5.points.0: 🗺️ **Parcel Mapping** — detailed records of soil, aspect, drainage and microclimate for every plot
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: 🧱 **The Clos System** — stone walls (clos) enclosing vineyards to delineate parcels of differing rank
lessons.1.slides.5.points.2: 🍇 **Precision Viticulture** — yield control, pruning techniques, and other refined growing methods
lessons.1.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 **Winemaking Technique** — recording how different methods affect quality and codifying best practice
lessons.1.slides.5.points.4: 📝 **Climat Naming** — a parcel-naming system giving every plot a unique name and history
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Legendary Estate: Clos de Vougeot
lessons.1.slides.6.caption: Clos de Vougeot, founded in 1110, is the Cistercians' greatest creation. The 50-hectare vineyard is fully enclosed by walls and remains a Burgundian landmark. Although now divided among more than 80 growers, it preserves its unified clos identity to this day.
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Famous Clos (walled vineyards)
lessons.1.slides.7.points.0: 🏆 **Clos de Vougeot** — Grand Cru, 50 ha, the largest single vineyard in the Côte de Nuits
lessons.1.slides.7.points.1: 👑 **Clos de Tart** — Grand Cru, 7.5 ha, jewel of Morey-Saint-Denis
lessons.1.slides.7.points.2: 💎 **Clos des Lambrays** — Grand Cru, 8.7 ha, almost a monopole
lessons.1.slides.7.points.3: ⭐ **Clos Saint-Denis** — Grand Cru, 6.6 ha, the embodiment of elegance and finesse
lessons.1.slides.7.points.4: 🌟 **Clos de la Roche** — Grand Cru, 16.9 ha, powerful and structured in style
lessons.1.slides.8.title: 👑 The Era of the Dukes of Burgundy (14th–15th c.)
lessons.1.slides.8.content: The 14th and 15th centuries were Burgundy's golden age. The Dukes of Burgundy ruled vast lands stretching from the Low Countries to Switzerland, at times rivalling the King of France in power. Wine-loving and ambitious, they used Burgundy's wines as diplomatic gifts, making them the favoured drink of European courts.
lessons.1.slides.9.title: 📜 The Historic Decree of 1395
lessons.1.slides.9.content:
On 6 July 1395, Duke Philippe le Hardi (Philip the Bold) issued an edict that would change Burgundy's destiny:

**"The planting of Gamay is forbidden, on pain of severe punishment."**

He called Gamay a très déloyal plant — a most disloyal vine — believing its high yields were eroding the quality and reputation of Burgundian wine. The decree imposed Pinot Noir on the region and established Burgundy's enduring tradition of placing quality before quantity.
lessons.1.slides.10.title: ⚔️ The Far-Reaching Impact of the Revolution (1789)
lessons.1.slides.10.content: When the French Revolution erupted in 1789, the property of the Church and nobility was confiscated and nationalised. Between 1790 and 1791 these vineyards were broken up into small parcels and auctioned to ordinary citizens, forging Burgundy's distinctive structure of land ownership.
lessons.1.slides.11.title: What the Revolution Changed
lessons.1.slides.11.points.0: 📊 **Land fragmentation** — vast estates split into hundreds of small parcels
lessons.1.slides.11.points.1: 👨‍🌾 **Birth of the smallholder economy** — farmers owned vineyards for the first time
lessons.1.slides.11.points.2: 🔄 **Generational subdivision** — French inheritance law divides estates equally among children, fragmenting parcels further with each generation
lessons.1.slides.11.points.3: 🤝 **A culture of cooperation** — small growers unable to vinify alone gave rise to the négociant system
lessons.1.slides.11.points.4: 🎯 **Quality focus** — small parcels actually sharpened the understanding of terroir
lessons.1.slides.12.title: 👥 Burgundy's Smallholder Marvel
lessons.1.slides.12.content:
Land ownership in Burgundy is extraordinarily fragmented — unique among the world's wine regions:

• **Clos de Vougeot** — 50 ha shared by more than 80 growers
• **Corton-Charlemagne Grand Cru** — average ownership of just 0.5 ha per holder
• A single Grand Cru may yield more than 30 different bottlings

This pattern explains why Burgundy is home to thousands of small estates, and why quality and price under the same vineyard name can vary so dramatically.
lessons.1.slides.13.title: 🏛️ The Birth of the AOC (1936)
lessons.1.slides.13.content:
In 1936, France established the AOC (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée) system, codifying centuries of Burgundian terroir wisdom into law.

The regulations strictly govern:
• Grape varieties (Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, etc.)
• Planting density and maximum yields
• Vinification methods
• Alcohol ranges

AOC ensures that the name "Gevrey-Chambertin" denotes far more than a place — it stands for an entire system of guaranteed quality.
lessons.1.slides.14.title: 🌍 UNESCO World Heritage: The Climats (2015)
lessons.1.slides.14.content:
On 4 July 2015, Burgundy's Climats were officially inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List — the highest possible recognition of a thousand years of winemaking culture.

**Climats** refers to 1,247 precisely delimited vineyard parcels, from Chablis down to Maranges. Each has:
• A unique name (often medieval in origin)
• A specific soil composition
• Defined boundaries (often marked by stone walls)
• Centuries of documented history

These Climats are not merely vineyards but, as UNESCO put it, a living testament to two thousand years of interaction between humanity and nature.
lessons.1.slides.15.title: Climat and Lieu-dit Explained
lessons.1.slides.15.caption: A two-fold geography: the administrative lieu-dit alongside the official Climat that embodies the soul of terroir.
lessons.1.slides.16.title: 📚 Historical Recap
lessons.1.slides.16.points.0: 🏛️ The Romans laid the foundations of Burgundian viticulture
lessons.1.slides.16.points.1: ⛪ The monks created the concept of terroir and a scientific approach to winemaking
lessons.1.slides.16.points.2: 👑 The Dukes of Burgundy mandated Pinot Noir, choosing quality over quantity
lessons.1.slides.16.points.3: ⚔️ The French Revolution forged Burgundy's distinctive smallholder structure
lessons.1.slides.16.points.4: 📜 The AOC system translated traditional wisdom into legal protection
lessons.1.slides.16.points.5: 🌍 UNESCO recognition of the Climats affirmed the universal value of Burgundian culture
lessons.1.slides.17.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.0.question: Which group contributed most to the development and mapping of Burgundy's vineyards?
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.0.explanat: The Cistercians and the monks of Cluny Abbey systematically studied, classified and mapped Burgundy's vineyards in the Middle Ages, laying the foundation of today's Climat system.
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.1.question: Which noble dynasty ruled the Duchy of Burgundy and made its wines famous across Europe?
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.1.explanat: The medieval Duchy of Burgundy was ruled by the Valois Dukes, who actively promoted Burgundian wine and exported it to courts across Europe, securing the region's international fame.
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.2.question: Which were impacts of the French Revolution on Burgundy's vineyards? (multiple answers)
A. Confiscation of monastic and noble vineyards
B. Vineyards split into parcels and auctioned to many buyers
C. All vineyards were taken into permanent state ownership
D. The hyper-fragmented ownership pattern still seen today
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.2.explanat: The Revolution (1789) confiscated and auctioned Church and noble vineyards. Parcels were broken up and sold to many small owners, creating today's extreme fragmentation — a single Climat may have dozens of co-owners.
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.3.question: What is the long-term effect of the Napoleonic Code on Burgundian vineyard ownership?
B. The principle of equal inheritance keeps subdividing the vineyards
C. It forbids the sale of land, preserving stability
D. It has had no significant impact
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.3.explanat: The Napoleonic Code requires that an estate be divided equally among heirs. Generation after generation, vineyards keep splitting. That is why DRC's Romanée-Conti, only 1.8 ha, has had so many co-heirs over the centuries.
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.4.question: What is the role of a négociant in the Burgundy wine trade?
B. A merchant who buys grapes or must, then vinifies and bottles the wine
C. A foreign company specialising in exporting Burgundy
D. The body that certifies Burgundy wines
lessons.1.slides.17.questions.4.explanat: A négociant plays a key role in Burgundy: buying grapes or must from many small growers, then vinifying and bottling under a single label. Bouchard, Louis Jadot and Drouhin are well-known négociant houses.
lessons.1.slides.18.title: 💡 Why Does History Matter?
lessons.1.slides.18.content:
Understanding Burgundy's history helps us see:

**1. Why quality matters more than quantity** — a philosophy carried forward from the 1395 decree.

**2. Why every parcel has a name** — a millennium of accumulated terroir wisdom from the monks.

**3. Why a single vineyard has so many estates** — the legacy of the French Revolution.

**4. Why Burgundy wines are so expensive** — the inevitable result of small parcels, low yields and high quality.

History is not the past tense; it lives in every bottle of Burgundy.
lessons.2.title: Principal Grape Varieties
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Principal Grape Varieties
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 — 15 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: An in-depth look at the two classic Burgundian grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: Burgundy's Single-Variety Philosophy
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Unlike Bordeaux's blending tradition, Burgundy is committed to single-variety wines. Reds are almost entirely Pinot Noir, while whites are predominantly Chardonnay.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Profile of the Two Soul Varieties
lessons.2.slides.2.caption: How Pinot Noir and Chardonnay express terroir, and a side-by-side stylistic spectrum.
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🍇 The Two Classics Compared
lessons.2.slides.3.grapes.0.name: Pinot Noir
lessons.2.slides.3.grapes.0.regions.0: Côte de Nuits — the very pinnacle
lessons.2.slides.3.grapes.0.regions.1: Côte de Beaune — elegant and supple
lessons.2.slides.3.grapes.1.name: Chardonnay
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 📊 Three Grapes — Style Radar
lessons.2.slides.4.content: A side-by-side comparison of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Gamay across flavour and stylistic traits.

lessons.2.slides.5.title: Why Pinot Noir Is So Special
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: One of the hardest grapes to grow — exquisitely demanding of climate and soil
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: Thin-skinned — vulnerable to disease and pests
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: An early-ripening variety — needs cool climates to retain acidity
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: Translates terroir like no other — often called "the transparent grape"
lessons.2.slides.6.title: Chardonnay's Versatility
lessons.2.slides.6.points.0: Highly adaptable — grown the world over
lessons.2.slides.6.points.1: Stylistically diverse — from crisp and mineral to rich and buttery
lessons.2.slides.6.points.2: Oak use — a key driver of the final style
lessons.2.slides.6.points.3: Burgundy is Chardonnay's spiritual home and global benchmark
lessons.2.slides.7.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.0.question: Burgundy reds are made almost exclusively from which grape?
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.0.explanati: Pinot Noir is the sole red grape of Burgundy, the source of its elegance and complexity and the defining variety of the region's style: high acidity, light body, fine aromatics — and one of the most challenging and most coveted grapes in the world.
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.1.question: Which variety dominates Burgundy whites?
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.1.explanati: Chardonnay is at the heart of Burgundy whites. From the mineral cut of Chablis to the buttery breadth of Meursault, it shows the variety's astonishing range across terroirs and stands as one of the world's greatest white grapes.
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.2.question: Which statements about Burgundy Pinot Noir are correct? (multiple answers)
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.2.options.0: A. Light tannin and a paler colour than Cabernet Sauvignon
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.2.options.1: B. Notable for high acidity and red-fruit aromatics
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.2.options.2: C. Old vines and great vintages can age for decades
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.2.options.3: D. Inky black, high in alcohol, best drunk young
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.2.explanati: Pinot Noir features light tannins, a pale ruby hue, high acidity and red-fruit aromatics. Top examples (Grand Cru) age extraordinarily well, but the colour will never reach Cabernet's depth — that is intrinsic to the variety.
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.3.question: Which grape is the mainstay of the Beaujolais region?
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.3.explanati: Gamay is the heart of Beaujolais, with red fruit, floral notes and a touch of earth, in a fresh and lively style. Wines from the ten Crus can even age, with greater complexity than typical Beaujolais.
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.4.question: Which other grapes does Burgundy permit? (multiple answers)
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.4.options.2: C. Merlot is also allowed in blends
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.4.options.3: D. Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc may be used in small quantities
lessons.2.slides.7.questions.4.explanati: Aligoté is Burgundy's principal secondary white, often as Bourgogne Aligoté AOC. Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are permitted in small amounts in white blends. Merlot is not allowed anywhere in Burgundy.
lessons.2.slides.8.title: Other Varieties
lessons.2.slides.8.content: Beyond Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Burgundy also grows small amounts of Aligoté (white) and Gamay (red, mainly in Beaujolais). Aligoté yields fresh, lively whites and is the base of the famous Kir cocktail.

lessons.3.slides.0.description: Learn to decode a Burgundy label, master the classification system and pick out the key information.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: What Makes a Burgundy Label Distinctive
lessons.3.slides.1.content: A Burgundy label may look simple, but it carries a wealth of information. Reading it is the first step to buying Burgundy wisely — and the key to understanding Burgundy's classification system.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🏷️ Essential Label Elements (top to bottom)
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: 2. Vineyard name — may include Grand Cru or Premier Cru
lessons.3.slides.3.title: The Four-Tier Classification Pyramid
lessons.3.slides.3.points.3: Grand Cru — only about 1% of production
lessons.3.slides.4.title: How to Identify the Tier
lessons.3.slides.4.content: Grand Cru — the label only carries the vineyard name, e.g. "Chambertin". Premier Cru — village name plus vineyard name, e.g. "Gevrey-Chambertin 1er Cru Les Cazetiers".
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🍷 Grand Cru Label Example: Chambertin Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.5.caption: A Grand Cru label shows only the vineyard name ("Chambertin"); no village name is required.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 🍷 Premier Cru Label Example: Gevrey-Chambertin 1er Cru
lessons.3.slides.6.caption: A Premier Cru label combines village + 1er Cru + vineyard name: Gevrey-Chambertin 1er Cru Les Cazetiers.
lessons.3.slides.7.title: Common French Terms on Labels
lessons.3.slides.7.points.0: Mis en bouteille au domaine — bottled at the estate
lessons.3.slides.7.points.2: Monopole — a vineyard with a single owner

lessons.3.slides.8.title: Buying Tips
lessons.3.slides.8.points.0: Beginners: start with Village wines — sensibly priced and reliably good
lessons.3.slides.8.points.1: Improvers: explore Premier Cru and feel the differences between parcels
lessons.3.slides.8.points.2: Collectors: Grand Cru rewards long ageing and serious investment
lessons.3.slides.8.points.3: Mind the vintage: Burgundy varies dramatically year to year, and price follows quality
lessons.3.slides.9.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.0.question: On a label that reads "Gevrey-Chambertin", what is being named?
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.0.explanati: Gevrey-Chambertin is a village in the Côte de Nuits. A village name on a Burgundy label denotes a Village AOC — better than a regional Bourgogne but below Premier and Grand Cru.
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.1.question: What does "1er Cru" or "Premier Cru" indicate on a label?
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.1.options.0: A. The wine was made in the producer's first year
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.1.options.1: B. A vineyard at the second-highest tier of Burgundy's classification
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.1.options.2: C. An honorary title for the founder
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.1.options.3: D. The wine was aged in the first oak barrel
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.1.explanati: Premier Cru is the second-highest of the four tiers (Régionale < Village < Premier Cru < Grand Cru). The vineyard name follows the village, e.g. Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses 1er Cru.
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.2.question: Which statements about "Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses Premier Cru 2018" are correct? (multiple answers)
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.2.options.0: A. The wine is at the Premier Cru level
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.2.options.1: B. Les Amoureuses is the vineyard, located in the village of Chambolle-Musigny
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.2.options.3: D. This is Burgundy's top Grand Cru tier
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.2.explanati: It is a Premier Cru, not a Grand Cru. Les Amoureuses is the vineyard (Climat), located in Chambolle-Musigny, and 2018 is the vintage. Outstanding though it is, Premier Cru still ranks below Grand Cru.
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.3.question: If a label reads only "Bourgogne Pinot Noir", what tier is this?
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.3.options.0: A. The highest tier, Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.3.options.1: B. Regional Bourgogne — the entry level
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.3.explanati: "Bourgogne" alone is a regional AOC — the most basic of the four tiers. Grapes may come from anywhere in Burgundy. Quality is approachable, the wine is for everyday drinking, and prices are the lowest.
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.4.question: What is the main difference between a Domaine and a Négociant in Burgundy?
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.4.options.0: A. A Domaine sells only white wine; a Négociant only red
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.4.options.1: B. A Domaine grows its own grapes and vinifies them; a Négociant buys grapes or finished wine from outside
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.4.options.3: D. Négociant always means higher quality
lessons.3.slides.9.questions.4.explanati: A Domaine owns its vineyards and vinifies its own fruit; a Négociant buys grapes or must from many growers, then vinifies and bottles. Domaine wines often show stronger parcel character, while négociants offer broader range and consistency.
lessons.3.slides.10.title: Domaine vs Négociant
lessons.3.slides.10.content: A Domaine (estate) owns its vineyards and makes its own wine; a Négociant (merchant) buys grapes or wine from growers and bottles it under its own label. Both have their strengths — and many négociants today also farm their own vineyards.
